items.title: Faurschou Ends Its Public Exhibition Program as Its New York Space Heads for Demolition
items.summary:
When Faurschou New York opened in 2019, the New York Times compared it to major collector-founded institutions like the Hill Art Foundation, the FLAG Art Foundation, and the Brant Foundation. But unlike those institutions, Faurschou New York was not a 501(c)(3) nonprofit. It also never quite lived up to its lofty expectations.

In March 2025, Faurschou, which was founded as a private art museum and art consultancy in Copenhagen in 1986, announced that the New York outpost was closed “for renovations.” It never reopened. The Greenpoint building that housed it was sold in June to a developer, city records show, and the city has approved its demolition. A condominium planned for the site cements what founder and art collector Jens Faurschou himself announced in April: After four decades, Faurschou’s public exhibitions are over.

The building at 148-150 Green Street, once home to Faurschou New York and the restaurant Ilis, was sold at the end of June to the developer Investmates for $25.55 million, according to city property records reviewed by ARTnews . The seller, Green Art Holdings LLC, bought it in 2017 for $18 million, according to Commercial Observer . On October 27, the Department of Buildings approved its full demolition, according to city records. Investmates plans a seven-story, 73-unit condominium on the site, Crain’s reported.

In a statement posted to the company’s website, Jens Faurschou said that with the closing of the New York space he was “bringing the public exhibition program to an end.” After 40 years, he wrote, his “direction changes”: He will focus on…
items.t: Faurschou Ends Its Public Exhibition Program as Its New York Space Heads for Demolition

items.title: Lynette Yiadom-Boakye and Anne Imhof Make Vogue’s 2026 Best-Dressed List
items.summary:
As the year comes to an end, it’s that time when glossy titles publish their annual best-dressed lists—actors and musicians are to be expected, naturally. On Monday, Vogue US and British Vogue published their lists simultaneously, featuring A-list stars such as Zendaya, Kendall Jenner, Greta Lee, Sarah Pidgeon and more. Artists were also named, although few and far among them were British painter and writer Lynette Yiadom-Boakye, artist and choreographer Anne Imhof, and architect Sumayya Vally.

Vogue US selected 55 individuals for its best-dressed lists, while British Vogue handpicked 50. Yiadom-Boakye and Vally made it to British Vogue ’s list, and Imhof was paired with her partner, the dancer Devon Teuscher, by Vogue US.

Imhof and Teuscher were described as “Berghain Romeo and Juliet” by Vogue US, and the publication said 2026 was their year because of Imhof’s queer, Shakespearean solo exhibition “House of Swans,” which features a four-act ballet. Last year’s Vogue US list featured artist and New York’s First Lady Rama Duwaji. Vogue US could not be reached for a comment at time of publication.

Serpentine CEO Bettina Korek and Lynette Yiadom-Boakye. 

Gareth Cattermole/Getty Images 

British Vogue ’s best-dressed list applauded Yiadom-Boakye for her “eclectic” style. The magazine compared the artist’s style to the characters featured in her portraits, where “clothes naturally play a crucial role,” but argued that “while the fashion that features in her art never feels too hooked to a particular time or place, the clothes in her real-world wardrobe couldn’t feel more…
items.t: Lynette Yiadom-Boakye and Anne Imhof Make Vogue’s 2026 Best-Dressed List

items.title: Orthodox Cleric Wanted in Connection With International Forgery Scheme
items.summary:
A 44-year-old man was arrested during an undercover operation into an art forgery scheme in Athens, Greece, on Saturday, November 21, exposing an international network allegedly overseen by a Florida-based Orthodox priest. The arrest subsequently yielded the discovery of 35 forged paintings falsely attributed to prominent Greek and international artists, among other valuables. 

The man, who remains unidentified to the public, was arrested on his way to make a sale to an undercover cop who posed as a client online. He had six paintings that he was going to sell to the undercover agents for €5,150 ($5,613). The investigation began in early October, when an art specialist tipped off authorities after encountering an online listing of two paintings attributed to famous 20th-century Greek expressionist George Bouzianis with counterfeit certificates of authenticity for sale.
items.t: Orthodox Cleric Wanted in Connection With International Forgery Scheme

items.title: Joni Mitchell Has Some News
items.summary:
In her song “A Case of You,” Joni Mitchell described herself as “a lonely painter / I live in a box of paints.” She has never been a particularly shy one. The famously elusive artist, who has pronounced painting her "first love" before music, makes plain statements in NEWS, a collection of political paintings. 

Conceived and designed by Mitchell, the book unfurls a scathing rebuke of recent Republican administrations in the United States. Twenty-three paintings are presented chronologically, with a handful created between 2001 and 2004 and the majority made in the last 18 months. Works from the Bush years show the Twin Towers aflame with a sinister face in the smoke or a bare-chested blonde woman who sits astride Osama Bin Laden’s shoulders.

More recent works feature Adolf Hitler with the letters "MGGA" ("Make Germany Great Again"), former DHS Secretary Kristi Noem on horseback labeled “grifter,” and a triptych of Jeffrey Epstein, Ghislaine Maxwell, and President Trump as disgraced royalty playing cards. A spread of all the works becomes a Thunderdome-like arena of modern US politics — ending with a self-portrait of Mitchell receiving a Kennedy Center Honor. As if the answer to all that chaos is elevating impactful art.
items.t: Joni Mitchell Has Some News

items.title: 13th-Century Carving Stolen by Art Thief ‘Eric the Belgian’ Recovered in the UK
items.summary:
Spain’s National Police have spent the past 47 years searching for a Romanesque wood carving of the Virgin Mary that was stolen from the Church of Sa Pedro de Meoz in Navarre, part of the Basque area of northern Spain. At last, they finally found it.

The 21-inch-tall gilded object was nabbed by the notorious “gentleman thief” René Alphonse van den Berghe, known as Erik the Belgian, who robbed churches and monasteries in rural Spain in the late 1970s and early ’80s. Many of his marks have since been recovered. In 2023, for example, a missing fragment from a set of six 17th-century Flemish tapestries was returned to the church in Castrojeriz, Spain, from where Erik the Belgian had swiped them in 1980.

As reported in El País , the investigation leading to this latest discovery picked up steam in April. The authorities knew that Erik the Belgian transported most of his loot from Spain to other European countries “with higher demand in the art and antiques market.”

The local paper Noticias de Navarra notes that in 2012 the Virgin sculpture was sold by a Belgian antique dealer named Bernard Descheemaker, and that by 2017 it was part of the collection Daniel Kanz Gallery in London.

In 2020, according to El País , it found its way to Maastricht in the Netherlands as part of TEFAF, the prestigious art and antiques fair organized by the European Fine Art Foundation. It then “passed through the hands of various antique dealers and collectors,” eventually landing with a Spanish art collection in the UK.

The handover took place at the Spanish Embassy in London, and the piece is…
items.t: 13th-Century Carving Stolen by Art Thief ‘Eric the Belgian’ Recovered in the UK

items.title: Friedrich Christian Flick, Art Collector and Scion of German Industrialists with Nazi Past, Dies at 82
items.summary:
Friedrich Christian Flick, a major collector of contemporary art and scion to one of Germany’s wealthiest industrialist families, died at 82 in Rosenheim in southern Germany. Flick died after suffering injuries from a fall days earlier, according to Monopol magazine.

Flick was a fixture of ARTnews Top 200 Collectors in the early 2000s, appearing on the list consecutively from 1999 to 2007. Flick’s collection is comprised of some 2,500 works, including major pieces by Bruce Nauman, Alberto Giacometti, Marcel Duchamp, Gerhard Richter, Georg Baselitz, Paul McCarthy, and Martin Kippenberger.

His patronage of the arts was not without controversy. His grandfather, Friedrich Flick, who died in 1972, was a top arms supplier to Nazi Germany and had built his company, which included production of coal and steel, on forced labor.

In 2001, Flick hired Rem Koolhaas to design a new museum to house the collection in Zurich. The project was met with protests both from writers and artists, as well as major Jewish groups, who criticized Flick for not contributing to a $6 billion fund for survivors of slave labor factories like those run by his grandfather.

The museum project was abandoned, and in 2003, Flick sought a new path for showing the works from the collection through a partnership with the Prussian Cultural Heritage Foundation, which operates Berlin’s museums. Flick loaned the collection for seven years to Hamburger Bahnhof museum and paid to renovate a 19th-century warehouse into an annex for the museum, as the New York Times reported at the time. According to Monopol , Flick…
items.t: Friedrich Christian Flick, Art Collector and Scion of German Industrialists with Nazi Past, Dies at 82

items.title: Trump Staffer Unwittingly Reveals Smithsonian Takeover Plan
items.summary:
With no sign of ceasing its attacks on the Smithsonian Institution , the White House could further upend the museum and research network, according to a supposed Trump staffer's documents for a tentative overhaul strategy, which were photographed on a Metro train in Washington, DC.

The photos, which a commuter took and dispatched to ProPublica , outline 25 items under the "Smithsonian Institution Renewal Plan," including the firing of National Museum of American History (NMAH) director Anthea Hartig, planned exhibitions on American nationalism, a redesigned logo and brand, and new institution-wide guidelines. If implemented, the measures could give the White House unparalleled authority over the Smithsonian's operations. 

While the identity of the staffer has not been confirmed, ProPublica 's report from today, November 23, speculates that it was Sam Bock, an associate policy adviser for the Trump-appointed Domestic Policy Council, which produced a draconian 162-page report in July that accused museum leadership, including Hartig, of promoting “extreme political activism."
items.t: Trump Staffer Unwittingly Reveals Smithsonian Takeover Plan

items.title: Mohamed bin Zayed University of Artificial Intelligence Launches $250,000 Art Commission Program
items.summary:
During Frieze Abu Dhabi week, the Mohamed bin Zayed University of Artificial Intelligence (MBZUAI) announced that it will launch a commission with a budget of up to $250,000. The task is to create a major sculpture or installation for the university’s Abu Dhabi campus.

The winning commission will be displayed in the university’s new cultural center that’s slated to open in 2027, and the artwork will be acquired for MBZUAI’s permanent collection. Artists applying for the commission can choose from one of three themes: the landscape, heritage, and communities of the United Arab Emirates; artificial intelligence and scientific inquiry; or the history between science and computation in dialogue with art, mathematics, and machines. 

“We shaped this open call as an extension of the collection we have built, which holds works spanning a century by artists who engage science through research, method and technique, treating knowledge as both an intellectual tradition and a material practice,” said Jasmine Soliman, head of art, archives, and special collections at MBZUAI, in a statement.

MBZUAI is building its art and special collections. The works in its inventory span from the 13th century for special collections and art collections dating to 1925. The university collects works based on the arts and sciences, as well as materials that document “the human pursuit of knowledge, creativity and research.” 

Dekyi (Hong) Liang, vice president and chief of staff at MBZUAI, said in a statement that it’s the university’s responsibility to “invest in cultivating a culture that embraces…
items.t: Mohamed bin Zayed University of Artificial Intelligence Launches $250,000 Art Commission Program

items.title: With MoMA, M+, and the Centre Pompidou’s Alliance, Museums Enter a New Era of Collaboration
items.summary:
If you are one of the world’s leading museums of modern and contemporary art, the story you are expected to tell has become global.

In the blink of an eye, it seems, the aperture of attention has snapped open to new world regions, publics, and technologies. Old narratives are yielding to a liberating, all-embracing polyphony. But this new story demands more, and different, art. Adding to the challenge, art prices are soaring, and so are operating expenses. As the museum pushes into the 21st century, reconfigured as a more open and inclusive enterprise, it must satisfy a host of novel and costly demands.

How do you keep up? You team up. That’s what New York’s Museum of Modern Art, Hong Kong’s M+, and Paris’s Centre Pompidou are doing. Announcing their new tricontinental alliance on October 30, they pledged to treat their collections as one. They are not tinkering around the edges. They are going into the heart of what it means to be a museum. Their goal is to kick the old habit of doing things by yourself, for yourself.

Why would institutions consider such a deep strategic alliance, and why now? Maximizing and leveraging the reach of individual collections is only the start. Museums are painfully aware that their current operating model is under strain. Governments, broke and distracted, are dialing back support. Philanthropy, generally still an American exception, has its own limitations. Earned revenues have plateaued. The room to maneuver is narrow. Doing more with less has become a shared predicament and imperative.

That’s the economic argument. But there’s more.…
items.t: With MoMA, M+, and the Centre Pompidou’s Alliance, Museums Enter a New Era of Collaboration

items.title: Did a Trump Staffer Accidentally Reveal White House Plans to Revamp the Smithsonian?
items.summary:
The Smithsonian Institution, which runs a network of nearly two dozen museums and research institutes throughout the United States, has been a target for president Donald Trump throughout his second term. The president and his staffers have criticized Smithsonian policies and challenged museum leaders, including hauling them to the Capitol to submit to openly hostile questioning from elected officials.

Now, nonprofit newsroom ProPublica has published a report saying that a man on a commuter train heading to Washington, D.C.—apparently a White House staffer—was seen working on a plan to drastically revamp the policies of Smithsonian Institution museums, including the Smithsonian National Museum of American History, in the nation’s capital, which has repeatedly come in for scrutiny.

The evidence? Another commuter’s photos of the staffer’s laptop, snapped over the man’s shoulder as he worked on it in the last week of October.

The “Smithsonian Institution Renewal Plan” comprises 25 items. They range from questioning specific exhibits the institution has organized to proposing to rewrite educational materials for schoolchildren and reviewing financial arrangements.

One item deals with a proposed permanent exhibit, to be titled “The Riches of Our Western Civilization Inheritance” and another on “Great Families of American History.” Outside the institution, says the document, should stand a “Colossus Statue” of George Washington.

New: A commuter spotted a plan to overhaul the Smithsonian’s National Museum of American History while commuting on a crowded Metro train. They…
items.t: Did a Trump Staffer Accidentally Reveal White House Plans to Revamp the Smithsonian?

The Venice Biennale, curated by the late Koyo Kouoh around the theme “In Minor Keys,” closed on Sunday, with Visitor’s Lions awards winners to be announced Tuesday.

The 61st edition, which opened May 9, was fraught with controversy, primarily over the inclusion of the Russian pavilion, but also the Israeli pavilion, both of which the Biennale jury excluded from the event’s prizes. The often-dubbed “art Olympics” nevertheless attracted 714,015 visitors, about a quarter of whom were under 26. The prizes were conceived as a replacement for the Venice Biennale’s traditional awards. However, some national pavilions have said that if they are selected, they would not accept it, in a show of unity with the jury, which resigned just prior to the Biennale opening. Now with Venice’s 2027 architecture biennale coming up, we’re…

items.title: Hauser & Wirth Now Represents Ser Serpas, Fast-Rising Artist Who Combs the Detritus of Everyday Life
items.summary:
Hauser & Wirth now represents Ser Serpas, a fast-rising artist known for her poetically minded installations and haunting paintings. Hauser & Wirth will represent the artist in collaboration with her longtime gallery LC Queisser, which has spaces in Tbilisi, Georgia, and Cologne, Germany.

She will have her first solo show with Hauser & Wirth at its Paris space in January. For that exhibition, Serpas will show a new series of paintings, as well as debut a multimedia installation. Born in 1995, she is one of the youngest artists to be represented by Hauser & Wirth, and one of a handful Latinx artists to show with the gallery, which added to its roster rafa esparza earlier this month. 

Born and raised in Los Angeles’s Boyle Heights neighborhood, Serpas is an itinerant artist who is primarily based in Paris but also “regularly moves between such cities as New York, Los Angeles, Geneva, and Tbilisi,” according to a release. Her practice is equally disparate, spanning various mediums from sculpture and painting to video and photography to poetry and performance.

Serpas is best known for her sculptures and installations in which she brings together the detritus of everyday life, giving the found objects that comprise them new life and meaning. She gathers the items from the streets where she is living or in residency. “I’m building a palette every time I go into a new city,” she has said of her process. In a 2023 New York Times profile , she described “Parisian trash [as] sturdy.”

To make her works, Serpas usually works alone, constructing the pieces in situ. She often tells…
items.t: Hauser & Wirth Now Represents Ser Serpas, Fast-Rising Artist Who Combs the Detritus of Everyday Life

items.title: Dylan Moran goes looking for trouble and disappears off the beaten track in this baffling comedy show
items.summary:
Royal & Derngate, Northampton
The Black Books star gets off to a promising start as he contemplates ‘the burning ball of what you don’t understand’ but his search for levity leads to half-baked ditties

Is Dylan Moran joking when he opens his show by telling Northampton’s audience “I didn’t write anything, or prepare”? By the end, you wouldn’t bet on it. Bleary directionlessness may be par for the course for the Irish comic, whose work has always combined poetic-philosophical dazzle with a certain wooziness. But after a promising start tonight, his new touring show, Looking for Trouble, conspicuously loses its way, as Moran frets about forgetting a significant chunk of material, before abandoning his encore and leaving a bewildered audience in his wake.

That’s a shame, because there are shards of trademark brilliance in the opening 20 minutes, which see the 55-year-old address himself, albeit obliquely, to the mysteries of being human in 2026, AKA “the burning ball of what you don’t understand” From Trump to AI, Moran surveys it all in wide angle not closeup, as symptoms of our confusion, atavism and fear of expulsion from the tribe. The quality of his thinking in this section, while cheerfully offering himself up as Exhibit A in this prosecution of humanity’s perplexity, is arresting. And there are zingers, too, including a word-picture of the genitals that, once heard, may never be forgotten.
items.t: Dylan Moran goes looking for trouble and disappears off the beaten track in this baffling comedy show

items.title: Miami Through the GTA VI Looking-Glass
items.summary:
Days before the Venice Biennale opened, the Golden Lion jury resigned amid calls to exclude Israel from the festival. Dozens of artists and pavilions took themselves out of the running in solidarity. Now, as the exhibition draws to a close, the Biennale is ready to present its visitors’ choice awards — a “poisoned chalice,” in the words of the Art Not Genocide Alliance (ANGA), that “few want to win.” ANGA reflects on a historic year of organizing against attempts to artwash Israel’s assault on Palestine in an opinion piece today.

As gamers everywhere pore over Grand Theft Auto VI , Senior Editor Valentina Di Liscia sits down with Miami-based artists misael soto and Leo Castañeda to make sense of the game’s many tensions and complexities, while Staff Writer Rhea Nayyar tracks down its various art references. In another form of uncanny valley, Associate Editor Phillip Pyle wanders through empty corporate offices in Midtown Manhattan, transformed by artists who dismantle the systems of technocracy from the inside out. More to start your week below.

—Lakshmi Rivera Amin, associate editor, books 

The Venice Biennale’s Sham Awards Cannot Artwash Genocide

Stripped of the silver and gold they wore in previous iterations of the Biennale, the new Lions have been thrown to the tourists; “Best Artist” and “Best National Pavilion” will be decided by a popularity contest. Why this surprising democratic turn? The expert jury initially appointed to give these honors resigned en masse in April of this year. These resignations were, in part, the result of the Art Not Genocide Alliance’s…
items.t: Miami Through the GTA VI Looking-Glass

items.title: Inside Edward Said’s World
items.summary:
‘Tis the season for great documentaries. Twenty years after the death of Palestinian literary critic and theorist Edward Said, a new film revisits his life and legacy. Moustafa Bayoumi, a student of Said himself, posits that it offers a new generation a glimpse of Said’s indomitable energy and inexhaustible fight. 

The lovely Eileen G’Sell takes a look at Trisha Ziff’s latest documentary, Frida: The Girl That Just Doesn’t Go Away, which screened recently at DOC NYC. The film considers the commercial afterlife of Frida Kahlo, asking how the artist’s personal history has been whitewashed even as her image circulates endlessly through retail culture. What happens when an artist’s legacy becomes as much a consumer product as a creative one? 

And finally, if you haven’t seen Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim’s You Can See Everything, what are you waiting for? It may be the best film I’ve seen all year, full of unexpected twists, turns, and glorious awkward pauses. Though billed as a documentary, the film raises what I think is a more intriguing question: Is Fielder a performance artist playing a documentarian? Not to toot my own horn, but I explore that possibility and more in my recent review, though be warned: spoilers abound.

—Rebecca Schiffman, associate editor 

Nathan Fielder Is a Performance Artist in Disguise

As an art historian, it’s hard not to relate what you see in everyday life to history — not in the sense that every lily pad recalls Monet or snowballs bring David Hammons to mind, but in the sense that sometimes art really does imitate life. This happened to…
items.t: Inside Edward Said’s World

items.title: Lucy Sante Talks About What Collage Enables That Writing Can’t
items.summary:
Lucy Sante started making collages long before she established herself as a writer of incisive theories of photography (see Walker Evans , from 1999, Evidence, from 1992, and 2009’s Folk Photography: The American Real-Photo Postcard 1905–1930 ); of urban studies (see Low Life: Lures and Snares of Old New York , her 1991 chronicle of the city’s underworlds); and of personal history (2024’s I Heard Her Call My Name: A Memoir of Transition ). As a teenage émigré in the 1960s, she would clip and assemble images from magazines, a practice she has continued on and off ever since—drawing lasting inspiration from the metaphysical juxtapositions of René Magritte, a fellow Belgian. As a clerk at the Strand, a storied used bookshop in New York, she began working with a wider range of materials, from cast-off paperbacks and technical manuals to medical textbooks and other arcane publications. All the while, she developed a mysterious and poetic style of collage that mixed imagery from different eras and suggested the outlines of stories, however elusive those might be.

Over the decades, Sante devoted herself most fervently to writing, with a focus on photography: In 2023, she retired as a professor of writing and the history of photography at Bard College. Her newest book, My Heart & I Agree (2026), is an essay collection that covers subjects including Surrealist photography, cowboy iconography, and Soul Train . There, her keen eye toward camera culture remains evident. She refocused some of her energies on collage in recent years, and her visual work featured this past spring in…
items.t: Lucy Sante Talks About What Collage Enables That Writing Can’t

items.title: Nine Night is back and proves itself a modern classic full of secrets, squabbles and laughs
items.summary:
Kiln theatre, London
Exquisitely acted, and directed with lightness and depth, Natasha Gordon’s 2018 tragicomedy about a Jamaican matriarch’s wake is moving and never mawkish

The death of a parent has a way of blowing up the lives of family members it leaves behind. The combustions of grief, greed and secrets revealed around a barely buried coffin litter the tragicomic works of playwrights such as Tracy Letts (August: Osage County) and Branden Jacobs-Jenkins (Appropriate).

You might want to add Natasha Gordon’s debut play to that canon, although it comes wrapped in its own distinct cultural tradition. Its structure revolves around the Caribbean funeral ritual that commemorates the death of a loved one over nine nights. A debut play written by a young Black British woman, featuring an almost entirely Black British cast, it got a huge reaction at the National Theatre in 2018.

Continue reading...
items.t: Secrets, squabbles and laughs bubble to the surface as a Jamaican family mourns in modern classic Nine Night

items.title: Lend them your ears! Julius Caesar is staged with just four actors – and a great big gong
items.summary:
Sam Wanamaker Playhouse, London
This truncated, candlelit version makes use of skilful percussion to occasionally fill in for oration but loses some of the play’s beauty and power

Any modern reformulation of Julius Caesar may inevitably be compared with Phyllida Lloyd’s innovative, all-female 2012 production, now revived by the Royal Shakespeare Company, which reimagined the tragedy as a play-within-a-play in a women’s prison.

This reworked version, adapted and directed by Joe Hill-Gibbins, does not match its depth and originality but certainly does something different. It is performed at 90 minutes straight-through with just four actors who take on the central roles of conspirators Cassius (Natey Jones) and Brutus (Caoilfhionn Dunne) alongside Mark Antony (Adam Gillen) and Caesar (Kate Duchêne, who also plays the soothsayer and Octavius). It is not as gimmicky as you may think.

items.title: Hail to the Squash King
items.summary:
Swimming in a Peter Bradley color field. Leaping from dot to dot on a Howardena Pindell speckled canvas. A Peter Jemison horse prances toward me. A Pepsi Cherry truck pulls over as I’m having deep thoughts about authenticity.

In the morning glow, a pretty woman walks down the sidewalk with a carton of a dozen eggs. A faded black-and-white Marilyn Monroe poster greets customers at the Organic Deli. A photo in the paper shows the presidents of the United States, China, and Russia against a giant painting of the Great Wall. A Madonna song whispers, “Express yourself, express yourself.”

A well-dressed man cycling to work is nice to look at. A Hilma af Klint painting sells for $12.7 million at auction, 16 times its highest estimate. Meanwhile at the supermarket, just three small items set me back $100. How could that be? If the middle class had any guts, they’d be out there on the streets burning effigies of Adam Smith and Sigmund Freud. But they’re not; they’re waiting 40 minutes in line across the street just to buy a bagel. 

At the Ace Hotel, I read something I’ve written for the new edition of The Other Almanac . I wear my heart on my sleeve in front of strangers. The next speaker is a whale necropsy expert. At the end of the evening someone is crowned “Squash King.”

A golden sunset falls over the glass towers of Long Island City. The Kosciuszko Bridge is lit with cotton candy colors. Fog in Downtown Brooklyn, or is it smoke? I can’t really tell. In Chelsea, I follow a group of people into an art gallery just to see what they’re into. It turns out to be a big mistake.…
items.t: Hail to the Squash King

items.title: Is GTA VI the Art Miami Deserves?
items.summary:
“Driving at rush hour. SIGNIFICANTLY less cars on the road.” The text was from Miami-based artist, educator, and organizer misael soto, sent yesterday, November 19, a few hours after the release of Grand Theft Auto VI . We’d come full circle: The bumper-to-bumper traffic that Miami, the city I once called home, is now notorious for — in no small part due to overdevelopment, climate change, and strained infrastructure — was being alleviated by a video game that keeps people at home, inside a simulation of the same city locked in time.

The premise of GTA VI is simple on the surface. The game follows Lucía Caminos and Jason Duval in the criminal underworld of Leonida, a fictionalized state based on South Florida: Miami becomes Vice City, the Everglades are the Grassrivers. But its portrayal of real-life hardships, socioeconomic inequality, and even Lucía and Jason’s love story, among other elements, has elicited deeper reflections and responses across our increasingly blurred online and physical worlds.

To help make sense of these tensions, I got on a phone call with soto and Leo Castañeda, two Miami-based artists whose work I admire. Castañeda is an artist and video game designer exploring Latin American Surrealism in the digital age, and soto co-leads Artists for Artists: Miami, which is leading a boycott of Art Basel next month, and works in the overlapping arenas of labor rights, public infrastructure, and conceptual and social practice. 

Our conversation was edited and condensed for clarity. I hope you enjoy it.

items.t: Is GTA VI the Art Miami Deserves?

A portmanteau of the Spanish words mal (poorly) and vestir (to dress), Malvestir features creatives across the Americas who probe the historical and contemporary resonances of Latin American dress. Western appropriations of Indigenous crafts, exorbitant textile waste, and the fetishization of Latin American styles are just some of the key concerns that will be interrogated in the exhibition.

Camila Falquéz's "Cello as Santa Barbara, Salvador de Bahia, Brasil" (2024) (© Camila Falquéz; image courtesy the artist and Hannah Traore Gallery) Curated by MoMA PS1 director Connie Butler and associate curator Elena Ketelsen González, Malvestir will include a range of artists, from New York City designers to textile artists reinvigorating intergenerational weaving traditions. 

Several designers are striving to reclaim styles and symbols co-opted by mainstream Western markets. Known for his oversized proportions and street-style designs emblematic of the Mexican-American fashion tradition, New York designer Willy Chavarria is showing Safe From Home (2024), a film that expanded upon themes of love and the right to safety explored in his Autumn/Winter 2024 collection. items.title: In a Midtown Office, Artists Sift Through the Junkspace of Capitalism
items.summary:
A few hours before 260 Madison opened on September 24, I trekked to its namesake address in Midtown to meet the curators. A security guard directed me to the 14th floor of the 1950s office building, where drop ceilings, an exposed HVAC system, and two people I assumed were the exhibition organizers dressed in corporate drag greeted me. They quickly clarified they were not ; they were from AmTrustRE, the real estate company that offered the derelict 23,000-square-foot office space to the artists for free while preparing it — and three other unoccupied floors — for their next corporate tenants. 

The three artists-turned-curators, Shaina Tabak, Dayana Matasheva, and Edson Niebla Rodríguez (the latter two of whom make up the duo DemonLovers Inc.), organized 260 Madison as an intergenerational, “inter-everything” show with work by over 50 artists, including self-taught and non-traditionally educated practitioners. On view through this Sunday, November 22, the show arrives just as the Whitney Museum of American Art opens artport: A History of Internet Art , signaling a new wave of institutional recognition for internet-grown art. With 260 Madison artists Maya Man, Rachel Rossin, and Eva and Franco Mattes among those included in the Whitney’s 25th-anniversary exhibition for its net art commissioning platform, the Midtown show feels especially urgent, if only because it takes place at the precipice of a paradigmatic shift within the art world.

items.title: The Venice Biennale's Sham Awards Cannot Artwash Genocide
items.summary:
This Sunday, the Venice Biennale will award its new “Visitors’ Lions.” But no matter who receives this poisoned chalice, the results are void. 

Stripped of the silver and gold they wore in previous iterations of the Biennale, the new Lions have been thrown to the tourists; “Best Artist” and “Best National Pavilion” will be decided by a popularity contest. Why this surprising democratic turn? The expert jury initially appointed to give these honors resigned en masse in April of this year. These resignations were, in part, the result of the Art Not Genocide Alliance’s (ANGA) nearly three years of campaigning to exclude the Israel pavilion from the art world’s most important biennial. After the jury publicly stated their intention to omit Israel and Russia from consideration for the Golden Lions, they were visited by representatives from Italy’s Ministry of Culture. The contents of the meeting are not public, but we can surmise how it went from the jury’s subsequent unanimous resignation. Shortly after, the Venice Biennale Foundation announced the Visitors’ Lions, inviting ticket-holders to cast their vote for awards to be announced at the end of the show’s run.

“Our exclusion has been thwarted, and the choice now passes to the general public,” crowed Israeli Foreign Minister Gideon Sa’ar, whom human rights groups accuse of orchestrating the siege of Kamal Adwan Hospital and the notorious imprisonment and torture of the hospital’s director, Dr. Hussam Abu Safiya, in 2024. Firmly siding with torture and against principle, the Biennale made it clear that both Israel and…
items.t: The Venice Biennale's Sham Awards Cannot Artwash Genocide

items.title: So You Want to Run an Artist’s Estate?
items.summary:
Much has been written about the “ Great Wealth Transfer ,” a predicted $80+ trillion phenomenon that will enrich younger generations as their parents pass away in the next two decades. For those who have inherited — or expect to inherit — the estates of visual artists, the challenges of this “transfer” can be especially complex. Works of art, which can carry both emotional and sentimental value alongside asset value, require special care and consideration. The resulting pressures and responsibilities can divide families and create legal challenges. 

For example, when the artist Sam Francis died in 1994, he left over 1,000 artworks, several businesses, extensive real estate holdings, ten cars, and a herd of cattle. His will provided money for a foundation called “The Sam Francis Museum,” but his vague instructions did not specify its activities. Disputes among his heirs — Francis had four children and had been married five times — and the need to extensively document his artwork further complicated matters. Settling all parties' claims and establishing the Sam Francis Foundation took nearly five years. 

The following text, which touches on topics facing estates, was developed in consultation with experts in fields that serve estates and trustees. There are also many organizations doing important work to advance this field, including the Center for the Preservation of Artists' Legacies, the Artists' Legacy Foundation, and Legacy Lab New Mexico.

Joe Oliveira, sole trustee of the Nathan Oliveira Estate Estate Planning Ideally, estate planning should begin while the artist…
items.t: So You Want to Run an Artist’s Estate?

items.title: Threading the Names of Alabama’s Black Belt History
items.summary:
AUBURN, Alabama — In Lowndes County, Alabama, less than an hour from Gee’s Bend, a group of women meet weekly to quilt together in a community center across from Mt. Willing Baptist Church. In 2021, they began to carefully stitch the names of formerly enslaved congregation members into their work. What started as a project to preserve and commemorate these forgotten figures of history soon grew into a broader collaboration across Alabama. 

Sew Their Names: Quilting, Creativity, and Activism at the Jule Collins Smith Museum of Fine Art at Auburn University culminates a three-year partnership between the university and the Hopewell Project . The exhibition showcases a series of handmade quilts by Yvonne Wells, Wini McQueen, and Mercedes Braxton, alongside fellow Lowndes County artists including Bill Traylor, Noah Purifoy, and Charlie Lucas, highlighting the region's rich artistic tradition.   

Mercedes Braxton poses with a recently completed quilt in front of “Oh Freedom,” on view at Auburn University (photo Stew Milne) “A lot of the time, when institutions are trying to connect with communities, they’re parachuting artists into a place that already has art and culture there,” Randi Evans, the former Manager of Public Practice and Community Partnerships at the Museum, explains. “We were really cognizant of our role, to work away from that narrative and work in collaboration with what was already happening at these sites.” 

A transplant herself, Evans hoped to learn about the traditions of Southern artists when she attended the quilt symposium “Every Stitch a Story,”…
items.t: Threading the Names of Alabama’s Black Belt History

items.title: The Real Miami Museums and Artists Behind GTA VI’s Vice City
items.summary:
After 13 agonizing years of waiting for Grand Theft Auto VI (GTA 6), gamers worldwide wasted no time tearing up the streets of the game's fictional state of Leonida after it was released yesterday, November 19. The South Florida-inspired game environment is heavily influenced by the culture, environment, and architecture of Miami — from its Art Deco resorts, white-sand beaches, Cuban quarter, and strip clubs, right down to its museums and arts venues.

As fans embed themselves in GTA 6's immersive landscape, many have recognized real-life locations across South Florida making unexpected cameos. One such case is the Vice Museum of Art, which Rockstar Games confirmed is modeled after the Bass Museum of Art in Miami Beach. 

“It was totally unexpected to see Grand Theft Auto VI reimagine The Bass as the ‘Vice City Museum of Art,’” said Silvia Karman Cubiñá, executive director of the Bass Museum of Art, in an email to Hyperallergic . 

“It’s a wonderful reminder of how art and architecture can become part of popular culture,” she continued. “Now, I’m just curious: will the Vice City Museum of Art get more visitors than we do?!” 

An exterior view of the Bass Museum of Art in Miami Beach, Florida, shows the clear resemblance to the Vice Museum of Art. (photo Robin Hill, courtesy Bass Museum of Art) While not listed as a landmark like the Vice Museum of Art, another building in Downtown Vice City appears to be directly modeled after the Pérez Art Museum Miami (PAMM). Situated near the Vice City Arts Center , which is heavily based on Miami's Adrienne Arsht Center for Performing…
items.t: The Real Miami Museums and Artists Behind GTA VI’s Vice City

items.title: A View From the Easel: Rei Xiao
items.summary:
Welcome to the 364th installment of A View From the Easel, a series in which artists reflect on their workspace. This week, Rei Xiao paints a world of surreal, feline figuration into being while navigating the artist visa system and managing their studio assistant (a dignified cat named Astrid).

Want to take part? Check out our  submission guidelines  and share a bit about your studio with us through  this form ! All mediums and workspaces are welcome, including your home studio.

Rei Xiao , Brooklyn, New York How long have you been working in this space? 

Two years.

Describe an average day in your studio. 

I work from my apartment. The most predictable parts of my studio day start with putting on my sunscreen and painting clothes. It’s a very small space that I paint in, so I usually have to push stuff aside when I start, like my painting cart, stool, and trash bin. 

I, then, turn on my air purifier, open the lids of my palettes, scrape paints from the previous session, and play either TV shows I’m familiar with or podcasts hosted by comedians in the background. The day usually ends with my cleaning the palette, emptying and wiping my brush cleaning tank, and diligently washing my brushes. Then I wash my face and go to sleep.
items.t: A View From the Easel: Rei Xiao

items.title: Ben Whishaw and Kathryn Hunter are a dynamite duo on the road to nowhere in Eurotrash
items.summary:
Young Vic, London
Adaptation of Christian Kracht’s novel is full of heartwarming comedy as a mother and son take a trip to distribute ‘dirty money’ to good causes

You would be hard-pushed to find a more charismatic double act than Kathryn Hunter and Ben Whishaw. She dazzles as a dowager, bringing flamboyant physical flourishes as she knocks back the cooking wine; he is her lugubrious son, Christian, a novelist with writer’s block. Their story trades on kookiness but the chemistry would keep you captivated even if they watched paint dry for the duration of this interval-free drama.

Based on Swiss author Christian Kracht’s bestselling novel, adapted by Colin Teevan, it is charmingly directed by Walter Meierjohann. The third big star is Lizzie Clachan’s set, so full of mischief that it is like a magician pulling out imaginative visual jokes and clever thrills and spills. Glyn Pritchard heroically plays ancillary roles (from taxi driver to waiter) with lightning-quick wardrobe changes while the sound effects are visibly, wittily created in a glass studio.

items.title: Hilma af Klint Is Rolling in Her Grave
items.summary:
Nothing in visual culture is neutral, least of all the color wheel itself. Scholar Richard Powell explores this deceptively simple truth in his new book, tackling the theoretical entanglement of race and pigment and how Black painters have used color over time. Trailblazing art historian Lowery Stokes Sims, formerly a curator at the Met Museum and director of the Studio Museum in Harlem, parses his richly layered essays today, linking the critical theory of Josef Albers and Darby English to the practices of artists like Jacob Lawrence and Alma Thomas. The book, Sims writes, shifted the way she’ll look at art moving forward.

Meanwhile, on the other end of the spectrum: News broke that a 1920 painting by Hilma af Klint sold for $12.7 million. Yes, the same Hilma af Klint who described herself less as an artist and more as a channel for a higher power, who followed the guidance of spirits that took physical form through her paintings. But hey, at least the painting’s owner has a new addition to their investment portfolio?

In reviews, Alina Cohen spends time with the poignant, impactful photographs by Laia Abril, who evokes the systems of patriarchy and sexual violence through the quietly haunting garments and objects in their wake. As the Cornell 7 case continues and convicted abusers sit in office, Abril’s photographs “reject both the invisibility of some crimes and the all-too-visible nature of others.” More, as always, below.

—Lakshmi Rivera Amin, associate editor, books 

Richard Powell Unsettles Race and Color Theory

items.title: Can depression really become dazzling dance? The biggest ever BalletBoyz show is a huge feat
items.summary:
Sadler’s Wells, London
In Six Lethargies, Iván Pérez and Seirian Griffiths have devised a mammoth production of aching, ethereal sadness

‘If I write what I feel, will you feel it, too?” That was the question behind singer-songwriter turned composer Keaton Henson’s Six Lethargies. Perhaps that is every artist’s mission, but for Henson it was specifically his experiences with anxiety and depression that he wanted to translate into music. Now it has been turned into dance by the BalletBoyz. If they dance it, will we feel it?

Six Lethargies is the largest production in the 25-year history of the BalletBoyz. Once just two ex-Royal Ballet dancers, Michael Nunn and William Trevitt, this iteration is a company of 44 dancers (male and female), a 37-piece string orchestra, and not one but two choreographers working together: former Dance Theatre Heidelberg artistic director Iván Pérez and talented newcomer Seirian Griffiths.

In Farah Ashraf’s solo show an obedient daughter secretly does online sex work as ‘PersianBaby’. The actor and writer explains how two worlds collide in her darkly funny play

At home, Amna is the modest and dutiful Muslim daughter of her parents’ dreams. Online, armed with a webcam and an OnlyFans account, she is PersianBaby – an exoticised version of herself complete with fake accent, designed to entice men willing to part with their cash.

Pink Rabbit, writer-performer Farah Ashraf’s provocative and darkly funny solo play, is a nuanced account of being caught between the private life of desire and the cultural expectations that shape how she is perceived. “I loved this idea of push and pull, and two different worlds,” says Ashraf who began work on the play during her final year at the Oxford School of Drama, before which she had trained with the National Youth Theatre.

In Briony Martha’s compelling play, a woman generates an alternative ending to her impromptu meeting with the Scottish superstar

Knowing what to believe is getting harder. Technology has blurred the line between truth and lies. Certain facts, though, we can demonstrate. We know, for example, that James McAvoy appeared in Cyrano de Bergerac at the Theatre Royal in Glasgow in the mask-wearing spring of 2022. We can also take playwright Briony Martha at her word when she says she bumped into the actor in a nearby coffee shop.

It is even true that McAvoy was in the audience of Martha’s Parasocial Activity towards the end of this summer’s run on the Edinburgh fringe: a performance that can only have had a heightened air of unreality.

items.summary:

Elliot Cowan is scarily convincing as the budding Potus in Donald, a high-speed, three-actor comedy from the playwright behind The Lehman Trilogy

His manner and actions often seeming like improbable caricature, the current US president sets a challenge for satire, any comic exaggeration likely to be trumped by reality. Mike Bartlett’s play The 47th (2022), staged between Trump’s administrations, pursued wild fantasies about the politician’s future career that were soon superseded by odder events. Ali Abbasi’s movie The Apprentice (2024) more sensibly focused on the period from 1973 to 1986 in which the New York realtor developed the behavioural and verbal tics that make him probably the most ridiculed figure in modern history, though such mockery, until the recent midterms, largely consoled detractors while being ignored by supporters.

Closer to Abbasi’s approach, Donald by the Italian dramatist Stefano Massini resembles his play The Lehman Trilogy – an international hit about the banking dynasty – in being a psychological analysis played by three actors with lightning switches of character and costume. items.title: ‘We can rage’: Michael Sheen fires up the gripping medieval epic Owain & Henry
items.summary:
Wales Millennium Centre, Cardiff
Sheen is in wondrous voice as Owain Glyndŵr, clashing with Henry IV, in Gary Owen’s stirring history play for Welsh National Theatre

No one does rousing like Michael Sheen. Whether urging on the Welsh World Cup squad or vowing “apocalypse” on The Traitors, he surges forward on waves of rhetoric. As Owain Glyndŵr, beacon of Welsh resistance, he doesn’t disappoint. “We can die gently and be forgotten,” he exhorts his followers. “Or we can rage.”

Rage and resignation, the sword and the song, resonate through Gary Owen’s absorbing medieval epic for Wales Millennium Centre and Sheen’s new Welsh National Theatre. Glyndŵr is a marginal figure in Shakespeare’s Henry IV plays, a thorn in the unstable king’s side. Here he stands central, a fitting protagonist for a moment of both surging populist politics and a disillusionment with power play.
